html:
Nur Jahan was the wife of the Mughal emperor Jahangir and, for about fifteen years, the real ruler of the Mughal Empire. No other Mughal woman held such power.

She was born Mehr-un-Nissa in 1577 at Kandahar, on the road, as her Persian parents travelled to India to seek their fortune. Her father rose high in Akbar's service. Her first husband, an officer in Bengal, was killed in 1607. In 1611 Jahangir married her, when she was thirty-four, and named her Nur Jahan, "light of the world".

Jahangir drank heavily and took opium, and he left more and more to her. She sat at the palace window to receive petitions, signed orders, and had coins struck in her name. Her father became chief minister and her brother a leading general. She traded with European merchants in her own ships and was a fine shot: she once killed four tigers with six bullets from an elephant's back.

In 1626 a general seized the emperor, and she planned his escape. When Jahangir died in 1627 she backed the wrong prince. Shah Jahan, married to her niece Mumtaz Mahal, won. She spent her last eighteen years at Lahore. The marble tomb she built for her father at Agra came before the Taj Mahal.
